checked_sources: Chi, Jung & Cauwenberghs 2010: full text opened from the authors' lab copy (isn.ucsd.edu/pub/papers/rbme10.pdf), DOI 10.1109/RBME.2010.2084078 confirmed via Crossref (IEEE Rev Biomed Eng 3:106-119). Malmivuo & Plonsey 1995: Chapter 13 opened at www.bem.fi/book/13/13.htm; publisher/year confirmed via the Oxford Academic record (academic.oup.com/book/25966).
evidence_location: Chi 2010, Section II (Skin-Electrode Interface), opening paragraph before II-A: 'the small signal amplitude of ECG (1 mV) and EEG signals (10-100 uV)'. Malmivuo & Plonsey, Section 13.1 Introduction: 'The amplitude of the EEG is about 100 uV when measured on the scalp, and about 1-2 mV when measured on the surface of the brain.' Neither source gives band-limited amplitudes, rms values, rhythm amplitudes, or anything about the spatial correlation of background EEG.
quote: especially given the small signal amplitude of ECG (1 mV) and EEG signals (10–100 µV)
discrepancy: Only the whole-signal figure ('scalp EEG as a whole is of the order of 10 to 100 uV') is supported, and even that loosely: Chi gives 10-100 uV, Malmivuo & Plonsey give 'about 100 uV', and neither says whether the figure is rms, peak or peak-to-peak (in the EEG literature such figures are usually peak-to-peak). The in-band default of 10 uV rms per electrode, the 1-30 uV slider range, and the spatial model ('independent cortical sources seen through the same lead field') appear in neither source, as the note admits. No arithmetic to recompute. Plausibility remark: if the whole-signal amplitude is 10-100 uV peak-to-peak, the broadband rms is roughly 3-30 uV and a decoder band a few Hz wide holds only a fraction of that power, so 10 uV rms in-band is at the pessimistic (high-background) end of the slider rather than a central value; the slider range covers the plausible values.
suggested_fix: Say explicitly that the two sources give the amplitude of the whole scalp EEG without an rms/peak qualifier, that the in-band rms default and its range are the site's own assumption, and that the spatial-correlation model is also an assumption not taken from these sources. If a source is wanted for the spatial statistics of background EEG, Nunez & Srinivasan, Electric Fields of the Brain (2nd ed., Oxford University Press, 2006) is the standard reference; for rhythm amplitudes in a band, cite a quantitative EEG source rather than Chi 2010 (an electrode review) or the textbook's one-line figure.
bibliographic_issues: Both entries have empty year parentheses and no venue. Chi YM, Jung T-P, Cauwenberghs G (2010), IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering 3:106-119. Malmivuo J, Plonsey R (1995), Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields, Oxford University Press, New York (ISBN 978-0-19-505823-9); the bem.fi URL is the authors' free online edition.

checked_sources: No sources are cited by the statement. Checked against: lecture slides following Kay, Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing Vol. II: Detection Theory (wuj.hosted.uark.edu/teaching/eleg5633/eleg5633_slides6_detection_deterministic.pdf; generalized matched filter, prewhitening, P_D = Q(Q^-1(P_FA) - sqrt(s^T C^-1 s))); Wikipedia 'Matched filter' (whitened least-squares interpretation); Duersch & Gu, arXiv:1509.06820 (QR with column pivoting, Algorithm 1); Crossref for Scharf & Friedlander 1994 (IEEE Trans Signal Process 42(8):2146-2157, doi 10.1109/78.301849).
evidence_location: Kay 1998 Vol. II, Chapter 4 (Deterministic signals), Section 4.4 'Generalized matched filters': statistic T(x) = s^T C^-1 x, whitening C^-1 = D^T D, performance P_D = Q(Q^-1(P_FA) - sqrt(s^T C^-1 s)), i.e. amplitude (deflection) SNR = sqrt(s^T C^-1 s). QR with column pivoting (Businger & Golub 1965; Golub & Van Loan, Matrix Computations 4th ed. 2013, Section 5.4.2): at each step the column with the largest trailing 2-norm is pivoted in and that norm becomes |R_kk| (arXiv:1509.06820, Algorithm 1 step 4). Subspace-interference interpretation: Scharf & Friedlander 1994, 'Matched subspace detectors'.
quote: the optimal linear filter for maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
discrepancy: none in substance. The derivation is standard: for a known pattern a in zero-mean Gaussian noise with covariance C, the Neyman-Pearson detector is the whitened matched filter and its output amplitude SNR is sqrt(a^T C^-1 a) (power SNR a^T C^-1 a). In whitened coordinates the noise is white with unit variance, so the matched-filter SNR of any vector is its 2-norm; the trailing norm that column-pivoted QR assigns to a pattern is the norm of its component orthogonal to the earlier (pivoted) patterns, which is exactly the SNR of the part of that pattern the earlier patches cannot produce, and equals the detectability of that patch when the earlier patches' amplitudes are unknown nuisance parameters (matched subspace detector). Three small points of wording: (1) under Gaussian noise the whitened matched filter is the optimal detector outright (Neyman-Pearson), not merely the best linear one; (2) sqrt(a^T C^-1 a) is the SNR only if a already includes the source amplitude (a = amplitude x lead-field column); for a unit-norm lead-field column the SNR must be multiplied by the source amplitude; (3) the per-patch residual SNRs depend on the order in which patches are taken, and column pivoting fixes a greedy (largest-residual-first) order, which should be stated.
suggested_fix: Add citations: Kay SM (1998) Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing, Vol. II: Detection Theory, Prentice Hall, Section 4.4 (generalized matched filter, prewhitening) for sqrt(a^T C^-1 a); Scharf LL, Friedlander B (1994) Matched subspace detectors, IEEE Trans Signal Process 42(8):2146-2157 for the 'part the earlier patches cannot produce' reading; Golub GH, Van Loan CF (2013) Matrix Computations, 4th ed., Section 5.4.2 for QR with column pivoting. Say 'optimal detector (Neyman-Pearson)' rather than 'best linear detector', state that a includes the source amplitude, and note that the per-patch SNRs are for the greedy pivot order.
bibliographic_issues: none (no sources cited; see suggested_fix for the references that should be added).

checked_sources: Stoica & Moses, Spectral Analysis of Signals (Prentice Hall 2005): full PDF opened from the authors' site (user.it.uu.se/~ps/SAS-new.pdf) and searched. Welch 1967: DOI 10.1109/TAU.1967.1161901 confirmed via Crossref (IEEE Trans Audio Electroacoust 15(2):70-73, June 1967); only the abstract could be read (IEEE Xplore page returned empty; index copy at search.isc.ac); the variance result is also summarized in Stoica & Moses Section 2.7.2. For the 2BT count itself: Shannon 1949, Communication in the presence of noise, Proc IRE 37(1):10-21 (reprint Proc IEEE 86(2):447-457, 1998), Section II, opened at web.cs.miami.edu.
evidence_location: Stoica & Moses: eq. (2.4.18) 'main lobe width in frequency f ~ 1/N' and Section 2.4 text '1/N is called the spectral resolution limit of the periodogram method' (resolution 1/T in Hz); Section 2.4.4 after eq. (2.4.34): periodogram inconsistent, variance does not fall with N; Sections 2.7.1-2.7.3: Bartlett averaging 'reduces the variance of the periodogram by the same factor L', Welch method, Daniell averaging over a band of width beta reduces variance by ~ beta N (= BT). Section 2.6.1 eq. (2.6.5) is a time-bandwidth product for windows (N_e beta_e = 1), not a sample count. Shannon 1949 Section II (Theorem 1 discussion): any function limited to bandwidth W and time interval T can be specified by 2TW numbers. Welch 1967 abstract: method averages modified periodograms of sections of the record.
quote: the periodogram is an inconsistent spectral estimator which continues to fluctuate around the true PSD, with a nonzero variance
discrepancy: Arithmetic is right: 2BT = 2 x 3 Hz x 1 s = 6, sqrt(6) = 2.449 (the site's '2.4' truncates; 2.45 would be the usual rounding). The 2BT degrees-of-freedom count is standard (Shannon 1949 Section II; Bendat & Piersol; Blackman & Tukey) and the periodogram facts attributed to the sources are correct, but neither cited source states '2BT independent samples' or an SNR gain of sqrt(2BT): Stoica & Moses give the 1/N resolution, the non-vanishing variance, and variance reduction in proportion to the number of averaged independent periodogram values; Welch 1967 gives variance reduction by segment averaging. Their 'time-bandwidth product' (eq. 2.6.5) concerns window widths, not sample counts, so it should not be cited for 2BT. Second, the sqrt(2BT) gain on the amplitude SNR is the coherent-integration result for a signal whose temporal waveform is known (matched filter over 2BT samples: SNR_out^2 = 2BT x SNR_sample^2). For an EEG feature with unknown phase/waveform (band power, event-related desynchronization) the detector is an energy detector; the band energy is chi-square with 2BT degrees of freedom and the deflection grows as sqrt(BT) on the power-SNR scale, which is a different number. The statement does not say which case the site assumes.
suggested_fix: Cite Shannon CE (1949) Communication in the presence of noise, Proc IRE 37(1):10-21, Section II (or Bendat & Piersol, Random Data, chi-square with n = 2 B_e T degrees of freedom) for the 2BT count; keep Stoica & Moses Sections 2.4.4 and 2.7 for the periodogram resolution/variance facts and Welch 1967 for segment averaging. State that sqrt(2BT) is the coherent gain for a known waveform (consistent with the matched-filter model in 'whitened-snr'), and that for band-power features the gain is sqrt(BT) on power SNR. Write sqrt(6) ~ 2.45.
bibliographic_issues: Years missing in both entries: Stoica P, Moses RL (2005) Spectral Analysis of Signals, Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River NJ (ISBN 0-13-113956-8); Welch PD (1967) IEEE Transactions on Audio and Electroacoustics AU-15(2):70-73. The Welch title and DOI are correct.

checked_sources: Wolpaw et al. 2002: full text opened (course copy at classes.engineering.wustl.edu/ese497/images/b/b3/2002Wolpaw_Review.pdf), DOI 10.1016/S1388-2457(02)00057-3 confirmed via Crossref (Clin Neurophysiol 113(6):767-791, June 2002). For the capacity formula (not attributed to Wolpaw): Shannon 1949 Section VII Theorem 2 (eq. 19, C = W log2((P+N)/N)) opened at web.cs.miami.edu; Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory 2nd ed., Chapter 9, Theorem 9.1.1 (C = 1/2 log(1+P/N) bits per transmission) and Section 9.3 (bandlimited channel, 2W samples per second) checked via lecture notes reproducing the chapter (di.univr.it matdid325610.pdf); Wikipedia Shannon-Hartley theorem page for the power-ratio convention.
evidence_location: Wolpaw 2002: abstract ('maximum information transfer rates up to 10-25 bits/min'); Section 4.9.3 'Assessment of both user performance and system performance' and Fig. 4 legend, p. 785 ('Information transfer rate in bits/trial (i.e. bits/selection) and in bits/min (for 12 trials/min)'); Section 5 ('maximum information transfer rates <= 25 bits/min'). Capacity: Cover & Thomas Theorem 9.1.1; Shannon 1949 Theorem 2.
quote: Current BCIs have maximum information transfer rates up to 10–25 bits/min.
discrepancy: The per-sample formula is correct: a discrete-time Gaussian channel with power ratio P/N has capacity 1/2 log2(1 + P/N) bits per channel use, and with SNR defined as an amplitude ratio P/N = SNR^2. Wolpaw 2002 does frame BCI performance in bits (bits/trial, bits/min) as the note says, and is not cited for the formula. The problem is the second clause, 'per window of T seconds that is the bits per second used here'. A band of width B observed for T s contains about 2BT independent samples (the site's own 'window-samples' claim), not one, so applying the per-sample formula once per window at the window-averaged SNR (SNR_w = sqrt(2BT) x s, giving 1/2 log2(1 + 2BT s^2) per window) is the capacity of a restricted scheme (one decision per window), not the channel's capacity, which by Shannon-Hartley is B log2(1 + s^2) bits/s with s the per-sample amplitude SNR. The two agree to first order at low SNR (both ~ BT s^2 / ln 2 per window) but diverge at high SNR: for B = 3 Hz, T = 1 s, s = 1 the site's expression gives 1.40 bits/s versus 3.0 bits/s. The site's figure is therefore a lower bound on capacity, and 'at most' is misleading for it. Also, 'per window ... is the bits per second' holds only for T = 1 s; otherwise divide by T.
suggested_fix: Rewrite as: 'A Gaussian channel with amplitude SNR s carries at most 1/2 log2(1 + s^2) bits per independent sample (Shannon 1949; Cover & Thomas 2006, Thm 9.1.1). We treat each T-second window as one channel use at the window SNR sqrt(2BT) s and divide by T; this equals the Shannon-Hartley rate B log2(1 + s^2) at low SNR and under-counts it at high SNR, so it is a conservative figure.' Keep Wolpaw 2002 (Section 4.9.3, Fig. 4) for the bits/trial and bits/min framing only, and add Cover & Thomas or Shannon 1949 for the formula.
bibliographic_issues: Wolpaw entry has an empty year and no journal: Wolpaw JR, Birbaumer N, McFarland DJ, Pfurtscheller G, Vaughan TM (2002) Clinical Neurophysiology 113(6):767-791. DOI correct.

checked_sources: Tangermann et al. 2012: full text opened at frontiersin.org (doi 10.3389/fnins.2012.00055; Front Neurosci 6:55; Crossref confirmed). Supporting: dataset description www.bbci.de/competition/iv/desc_2a.pdf (trial timing, evaluation rule), winner's entry description bbci.de/competition/IV/results/ds2a/KaiKengAng_desc.pdf, and Ang et al. 2012 Front Neurosci 6:39 (per-subject kappas, Table 2). Wolpaw et al. 2002: full text opened (course copy at classes.engineering.wustl.edu), formula in Fig. 4 legend p. 785 / Section 4.9.3.
evidence_location: Tangermann 2012 Section 5.5 'Outcome in brief' and Table 3: winner K. K. Ang, kappa 0.57 (others 0.52, 0.31, 0.30, 0.29); Section 5.2.2: fixation cross at t = 0 s, cue at t = 2 s, imagery 'until the fixation cross disappeared from the screen at t = 6 s', followed by 'a short break' of unstated length; Section 5.4: confusion matrix 'for each time point', 'The algorithm achieving the largest kappa value was declared the winner.' Ang et al. 2012 abstract/Table 2: mean kappa 0.569, classification output computed 'from the previous 2 s of EEG data'. Wolpaw 2002 Fig. 4 legend p. 785: B = log2 N + P log2 P + (1-P) log2[(1-P)/(N-1)], attributed to Pierce (1980) and Shannon & Weaver (1964).
quote: The performance measure kappa was 0.57 averaged over all nine subjects.
discrepancy: Recomputed: for N = 4 with balanced classes, accuracy = 1/N + kappa (1 - 1/N) = 0.25 + 0.75 x 0.57 = 0.6775 ~ 0.68 (the accuracy is derived, not stated in the source; the conversion assumes balanced class and output marginals). Wolpaw's formula with P = 0.6775 gives 0.582 bits/trial, i.e. 0.145 bits/s over 4 s; with the rounded P = 0.68 it gives 0.588 (0.147 bits/s); with the winner's published 0.569 it gives 0.580. So 'about 0.59' is a rounding artefact of using 0.68; 0.58 is the better figure, and 'about 0.15 bits/s' holds either way. Two caveats on the inputs rather than the arithmetic: (1) '4 s trials' is the motor-imagery period (t = 2-6 s); a whole trial including fixation and break is about 8 s, over which the rate would be about 0.07 bits/s; (2) the 0.57 is the maximum of a kappa time course computed per time point from 2-s sliding windows (competition rule 'largest kappa value'; winner's description 'computing the maximum kappa value'), so it is a peak value at the best latency, not a fixed decision after 4 s, and, as the note says, the winning algorithm's mean over nine subjects rather than a typical user.
suggested_fix: Write 'about 0.58 bits per trial (0.15 bits/s over the 4 s motor-imagery period)' and compute from kappa directly; say '4 s of motor imagery per trial' rather than '4 s trials', and add that the kappa is the peak of the time course for the winning algorithm, so the rate is an optimistic figure for that dataset. The formula's assumptions (equiprobable classes, errors spread evenly over the other N-1 classes) are stated in Wolpaw 2002 Section 4.9.3 and could be mentioned.
bibliographic_issues: Years missing in both entries: Tangermann M et al. (2012) Frontiers in Neuroscience 6:55; Wolpaw JR et al. (2002) Clinical Neurophysiology 113(6):767-791. Author lists and DOIs are correct.
